newsitem.title: USA: Nets Inc. files bankruptcy protection.
newsitem.headline: Nets Inc. files bankruptcy protection.

text.p: Internet commerce company Nets Inc., led by former Lotus Development Corp. Chief Executive Jim Manzi, said Friday it filed for bankruptcy protection because it could not get enough long-term financing.

The company said it will shut down most of its operations but will maintain its Industry.net Web site as it examines its options for reorganizing under Chapter 11 of the federal bankruptcy laws. In Chapter 11 a company is protected from creditors as it tries to work out a plan to pay its debts.

Formed through the merger of AT&T Corp.'s new media services and Industry.net in June 1995, the company has offered buyers and sellers of industrial goods and services a site to do business on the Internet since September 1994.

"This decision ... culminates 14 months of frustration for me," Manzi said in a statement. "As I said on the day I made my initial investment in this company, there is a great busines concept here with great potential."

Manzi said in a statement that in the past few weeks he has personally provided short-term loans to the closely held company. A company spokesman said work on a reorganization plan would start next week.
AT&T is a minority investor and Manzi owns less than 5 percent of the company, which is based in Cambridge, Mass. Nets has about 200 employees and an office in Pittsburgh.
Manzi stayed with Lotus Development for a few months after it was acquired in 1995 by International Business Machines Corp. and later joined Industry.net.

"Nets bit off far more than a start-up can chew," said Bill Doyle, a senior analyst with Cambridge, Mass.-based Forrester Research. "They had an impossibly broad objective. I think it was just too audacious for a start-up company."

He said the company's Industry.net was a good product which has been surpassed by technological advances. Also, IBM, and regional Bell telephone companies are now competing in the electronic commerce arena.
"There's a lot of big boys playing in this space and eyeing this same pie," he said.
